query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing surface segregation of Cu in the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating (via a tailored heat treatment) promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, lubricious Cu‐oxide layer during high‐temperature sliding. This oxide layer reduces adhesive wear and favors grain-boundary–mediated deformation, resulting in improved overall wear resistance and milder microscopic deformation compared to a baseline, homogeneous coating.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin coating with a nominally homogeneous solid‐solution microstructure on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition heat treatment designed to promote Cu segregation at the surface (thereby enhancing its oxidation) relative to the baseline as-deposited coating
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests performed at temperatures in the range of approximately 300–600 °C, under a controlled load and sliding speed
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Cu-oxide layer (likely CuO and/or Cu2O) at the coating's surface
generation.mechanism: The elevated temperature and engineered surface chemistry drive preferential oxidation of segregated Cu. The resulting lubricious oxide film minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, reduces adhesive wear during sliding, and shifts the underlying deformation mechanism from dislocation‐mediated plasticity to a more benign grain-boundary–mediated mode
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with enhanced surface Cu segregation and consequent Cu-oxide formation will exhibit lower friction coefficients, reduced wear rates, and less severe microscopic deformation (e.g., fewer and less pronounced intergranular fractures) compared to untreated, homogeneous coatings
generation.baseline: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a uniform elemental distribution and no deliberate enhancement of surface Cu segregation
generation.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold under conditions where the operating temperature is high enough (∼300–600 °C) to drive oxidation but not so high as to cause rapid oxide spallation; at lower temperatures the oxidation kinetics may be too slow, while at excessively high temperatures the oxide film may lose integrity
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, stability, and protective capability of the Cu-oxide layer can vary with ambient oxygen partial pressure and temperature; quantitative differences in wear rate and friction will require experimental validation to pin down their magnitude

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same substrate: one set undergoes a post-deposition heat treatment intended to induce Cu segregation, and the other is maintained as-deposited (baseline). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., at 400 °C, with a fixed load and sliding speed).
measurements: Quantitative friction coefficient measurements via a tribometer
Wear rate determination (via profilometry or mass loss analysis)
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS or Auger spectroscopy) to confirm the presence and continuity of the Cu-oxide layer
Microscopic examination (SEM/TEM) of the wear tracks to evaluate the deformation mode
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rates, or if surface analysis fails to detect a continuous, lubricious Cu-oxide layer (with corresponding changes in microscopic deformation), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

System: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each of Cr, Co, Fe, Mn, Ni). Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
